title: Economic Outlook 2025 - PwC
content:
According to the latest projections from the PwC Network, global economic growth is expected to ease slightly to 2.6% in both 2025 and 2.5% in 2026, down from 2.8% in 2024. This moderation is largely due to ongoing geopolitical tensions and rising protectionist policies. The US economy is forecast to expand by just over 2%, while China’s growth is set to slow to around 4.6%. The eurozone is projected to experience subdued growth, with GDP rising by 0.9% in 2025 and edging up to 1.4% in 2026 as [...] 8 Min Read 26/03/25 #### Economic Outlook 2025 The latest global projections from the PwC Network suggest global growth to remain moderate, at 2.6% in 2025 and 2026, with the US economy expected to grow at just over 2% and China’s growth moderating to around 4.5%. Growth is expected to remain slow in the eurozone, at 1.1% in 2025, picking up marginally to 1.3% as the German economy recovers somewhat. Meanwhile India’s economy remains robust, with growth expected to be over the 6% mark. Within [...] Global Growth Outlook

Global GDP growth stabilised at 2.8% in 2024 but is projected to decline to 2.6% in 2025 and 2026 due to geopolitical tensions and rising protectionism. The US and China are expected to slow, while India maintains strong growth above 6%.

Economic Outlook
================

Global Growth Outlook

Global GDP growth stabilised at 2.8% in 2024 but is projected to decline to 2.6% in 2025 and 2026 due to geopolitical tensions and rising protectionism. The US and China are expected to slow, while India maintains strong growth above 6%.

Impact of US Tariffs

The reintroduction of US trade tariffs led to downward revisions in euro area growth forecasts. The European Commission now expects eurozone GDP to grow by just 0.9% in 2025, down from 1.3%, with Austria seeing the sharpest downgrade to -0.3%.

Malta’s Economic Performance

Economic growth has stayed ahead of the euro area, but the pace is starting to show signs of slowing, with 2025 Q1 growth at 3.0%, following 3.1% growth in 2024 Q4 _._

Local economic sentiment

Malta observed a downward trend throughout 2024. Following a brief rebound in October and November, sentiment continued on its downward trend throughout the first five months of 2025.

#### **Global growth stabilised at 2.8% in 2024, expected to decline to 2.6 % and 2.5% over the next two years on the back of slower growth in US and China.**

According to the latest projections from the PwC Network, global economic growth is expected to ease slightly to 2.6% in both 2025 and 2.5% in 2026, down from 2.8% in 2024. This moderation is largely due to ongoing geopolitical tensions and rising protectionist policies. The US economy is forecast to expand by just over 2%, while China’s growth is set to slow to around 4.6%. The eurozone is projected to experience subdued growth, with GDP rising by 0.9% in 2025 and edging up to 1.4% in 2026 as Germany begins to recover. In contrast, India is expected to maintain strong momentum, with growth exceeding 6%. Against this backdrop, Malta’s 6% growth in 2024 and its projected 4% growth over the next two years stand out as comparatively strong.

**Update to projections following the Introduction of the US Tariffs as at 5 April.**

**The EC is predicting a slowdown in economic growth in FY25 due to the impact of the tariffs, with the euro area GDP forecast to grow at 0.9% in 2025 compared to 1.3% at the start of the year.**

The European Commission’s Spring 2025 forecast marked a clear shift in tone, revising GDP growth projections downward across the EU in response to new US trade tariffs. Austria saw the steepest cut from 1.0% to -0.3% while the euro area’s outlook dropped from 1.3% to 0.9%, highlighting regional vulnerability to global trade tensions.

Germany’s downgrade of 0.7 points underscored its export dependence. Malta’s revision was modest, from 4.3% to 4.1%, reflecting relative resilience due to its service-based economy. Spain, meanwhile, saw a slight upgrade, supported by strong domestic demand and investment momentum. Overall, the revisions signal a more cautious EU outlook shaped by shifting trade dynamics.

#### [](https://www.pwc.com/mt/en/publications/economic-outlook/2025-q2.html)**Malta’s economic growth has stayed ahead of the euro area, but the pace is starting to show signs of slowing _._**

In Q1 2025, Malta’s year-on-year growth slowed to 3.0%, similar to the 3.1% growth rate observed in 2024 Q4 and continuing a downward trend from the comparatively higher rates achieved in previous quarters in 2023 and 2024. In contrast, the euro area showed signs of recovery, with growth rising to 1.5%, its strongest pace in over a year. While Malta still outpaces the EU average, the gap is narrowing as domestic momentum softens and the eurozone gradually rebounds.

#### **When focusing specifically on 2025Q1 performance, trends mirror the broader annual expenditure patterns. The restaurants and hotels sector continued to lead with strong growth, while personal care and social protection registered a notable year-on-year decline.**

In Q1 2025, Malta’s strongest consumption growth remained in restaurants and hotels, which posted a 17% year-on-year increase, only slightly below the 18% recorded in Q1 2024. Education and communication also gained momentum, accelerating to 13% and 11% respectively. Housing and energy also picked up, while food and beverage remained stable.

However, several categories showed signs of weakening. Personal care & social protection moved from stagnant growth to a 6% decline, whilst the Transport sector which saw 14% growth in q1 2024 registered a modest 4% growth. These shifts suggest that while spending in essential and experience-driven categories remains resilient, broader household consumption is beginning to soften.

#### **From a GVA perspective, the positive growth observed in the Maltese economy is largely driven by externally oriented sectors such as financial services, while domestically focused sectors like construction and manufacturing show signs of weakening. Wholesale and retail trade also contributed positively, reflecting mainly the positive performance of hotels and restaurants which are included in this sector.**

Compared to the same quarter last year, Malta’s Q1 2025 GVA data reveals a shift in momentum across sectors. Financial and insurance services saw the strongest year-on-year gain, jumping from 1.5% to 10.6%, while wholesale and retail also strengthened to 8.5%. ICT returned to growth, and the public sector remained stable.

However, professional services and real estate slowed sharply, and both construction and manufacturing slipped into contraction. Arts, entertainment, and recreation (including gaming) remained in negative territory for the second consecutive year, pointing to persistent challenges in that segment.

#### **Meanwhile, growth in consumption per person remained flat in Q1 2025, compared to a CAGR of 3.4% over the 2019-2024 period.**

![Image 29: Graph explains economic outlook](https://www.pwc.com/mt/en/economic-outlook/GDP2.png)

Real private consumption per capita in Malta showed no growth in Q1 2025, remaining virtually flat at €3,750 compared to €3,749 in Q1 2024. This stagnation marks a clear pause in the upward momentum seen between 2019 and 2024, when consumption rose steadily at a CAGR of 3.4%. The lack of movement signals early signs of a slowdown in household spending and raises concerns about consumer confidence heading into the rest of the year.

#### Local economic sentiment in Malta observed a downward trend throughout 2024. Following a brief rebound in October and November, sentiment continued on its downward trend during the first half of 2025.

![Image 30: Graph explains economic outlook](https://www.pwc.com/mt/en/economic-outlook/graph%20q2.png)

The Economic Sentiment Indicator (ESI) continued to decline in 2025, following a temporary increase from the two-year low observed in September 2024. Despite a notable rebound in November above the 100 long-term average, the downward trajectory resumed into 2025, reflecting persistent concerns over economic uncertainty and a more pessimistic outlook for early 2025. The Employment Expectation Indicator (EEI) stabilized above the 100 average at the beginning of 2025, yet overall remained on a downward trend.

Conclusion
----------

Malta’s economic performance in Q1 2025 suggests a moderation in momentum. Real private consumption per capita during this quarter was flat year-on-year, signaling a pause in household spending growth after several years of gradual increases. Sectoral data reveals a mixed picture: externally oriented sectors such as financial services continued to expand, while domestically focused industries like construction and manufacturing contracted. Wholesale and retail trade also contributed positively, reflecting the continued outperformance in hotels and restaurants. Meanwhile, the Economic Sentiment Indicator continued its downward trend into the first half of 2025, reinforcing concerns about weakening consumer and business confidence. These developments suggest that while Malta remains relatively resilient, sustaining growth in future will require improvements in performance of the more productive sectors of the economy.

Here are the three key themes that will shape global economy in 2025:

============================================

In our Key Themes 2025 series, we share our thoughts on the key aspects shaping the outlook for global, regional, industry and city economies, highlighting opportunities and risks that you should monitor closely as you formulate your strategies.

#### Global economic outlook for 2025

Global growth is highly likely to hold steady next year, but beneath the surface the new US administration and China’s struggles are set to usher in a new, more mercantilist era for the global economy. Trade disruption, volatility in prices, and a new policy mix will determine the winners and losers in 2025.

Here are the three key themes that will shape global economy in 2025:

1.   US exceptionalism will come at a cost for the rest of the world
2.   Higher, more volatile prices become the norm as globalisation grinds to a halt
3.   A new and uncertain policy mix as fiscal and trade policy – not monetary – take centre stage

#### US economic outlook for 2025

US per capita GDP growth was the third strongest among advanced economies in 2023 and is poised to be among the best performers in 2024. With the heighted policy uncertainty and volatility in the bond market, can the US sustain its economic edge in 2025?

Download our report to explore the five key questions shaping the US economic outlook for 2025.

2.   Is the investment boom set to continue?
3.   How will fiscal and monetary policy evolve?
4.   What are the implications of less immigration and tariffs on growth and inflation?
5.   Will 2025 be the year of bond market volatility?

#### Asia economic outlook for 2025

While the fear of US tariffs has surged, China’s fiscal response to its ongoing slowdown is yet to arrive. Meanwhile, financial markets have already reacted, with Asian currencies depreciating and bond yields rising. Most likely, 2025 could well be a year of slower growth and more stubborn inflation than most believe.

Download our report to explore the four key questions shaping the economic outlook for Asia in 2025:

1.   What factors will influence Asia’s economic outlook in 2025?
2.   How will China navigate its economic challenges, and what impact could this have on the region?
3.   Is the optimism surrounding India’s economic outlook justified? Could India benefit from Trump’s China policy?
4.   To what extend will the rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI) benefit Taiwan, South Korea and Malaysia, and will this trend endure?

G lobal economic activity is expected to maintain modest but uneven momentum. We project that global real GDP growth will decelerate to around 3.0% in 2025 and 2.9% in 2026, following a 3.2% advance in 2024, as rising trade frictions, persistent geopolitical and policy uncertainty, elevated market volatility, and inflation divergence reshape the global outlook. Regional growth patterns have become more fragmented, with developed markets losing steam and emerging markets showing varied resilience.

In developed markets, real GDP growth is expected to moderate to around 1.3% in 2025 and 2026, following a 1.8% advance in 2024. The US economy will no longer be the outperformer, with real GDP growth expected to decelerate from 2.8% in 2024 to 1.5% and 1.3% in 2025 and 2026, respectively. The impact of higher tariffs will be on full display in coming months with subdued private sector sentiment, higher inflation, softening labor market conditions, margin pressures, reduced business investment and weakening consumer demand.

In Europe, a fragile recovery is underway, buoyed by disinflation and real income gains along with stronger fiscal tailwinds. However, the imposition of US tariffs along with rising policy uncertainty will constrain the upside for business investment and exports. We project euro area growth to remain subdued around 1.0% in 2025 and 1.3% in 2026 with disparities across economies. Japan’s economic recovery also remains modest, with GDP growth projected at 0.7% in 2025, following a 0.1% advance in 2024. While steady wage gains and a gradual rebound in consumer spending offer support, we expect external headwinds from trade tensions and structural challenges will continue to weigh on momentum.

We project global inflation to ease further in 2025, though progress will be uneven. For economies imposing tariffs, such tariffs will act as a supply shock feeding inflationary pressures. In contrast, the duties will act as a negative demand shock and weigh on inflation in tariffed economies. While headline inflation in developed markets is gradually retreating toward central bank targets, we forecast increasing inflation divergence between the US experiencing a tariff-induced inflation reacceleration and other economies experiencing ongoing disinflation. Emerging markets continue to grapple with localized cost pressures and currency volatility, especially where monetary policy easing is constrained, but Asia should experience ongoing disinflation. Overall, global inflation is forecast to decline from 4.5% in 2024 to around 3.6% in 2025, though downside progress remains vulnerable to commodity shocks, trade frictions, foreign exchange volatility and supply constraints.

Monetary policy is entering a new phase of divergence. While the disinflation trend has allowed central banks to pivot toward easing, the pace and scale of rate cuts will vary widely. The Federal Reserve is expected to proceed very cautiously, amid upside inflation risks tied to tariffs. The European Central Bank has eased more decisively and is expected to ease policy further through 2025 while the Bank of Japan (BoJ) continues its slow policy normalization and is expected to gradually tighten policy into 2026. In emerging markets, policy stances are increasingly reactive. While India, Mexico and South Korea are cautiously easing to support demand, others like Brazil, Nigeria and Turkey are maintaining or tightening policy to anchor inflation and stabilize financial conditions amid ongoing volatility.

Fiscal policy is increasingly constrained by high debt, rising interest costs, and political pressure for social spending, tax relief and defense outlays. While some governments are tightening, others are expanding to counter social unrest or weak growth. In Europe, Germany is pivoting from fiscal restraint, increasing spending on industry, defense, infrastructure and energy, even amid political tensions over debt limits. At the EU level, there’s growing support for loosening fiscal rules to enable long-term investment. Shifting electoral dynamics and political fragmentation further complicate durable fiscal planning across many economies. The implications for interest rates are significant. Higher debt levels and persistently large deficits are increasing debt servicing costs and pushing up term premiums, particularly in economies with shorter debt maturities or lower fiscal credibility. Even as disinflation allows for monetary easing, real long-term yields are likely to remain elevated, reflecting structural fiscal pressures and reduced policy space.

[](https://www.ey.com/en_us/insights/strategy/global-economic-outlook)Global economic outlook: reshaping growth and strategy via six themes
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The midpoint of 2025 finds the global economy in a precarious yet resilient state, navigating a volatile mix of macroeconomic headwinds and structural shifts. Momentum has broadly held, but growth trajectories are diverging more sharply across geographies and sectors. Mounting policy uncertainty — driven by a global reordering of trade relationships, financial market repricing and evolving fiscal priorities — is compounding the complexity of strategic planning. Businesses are operating in an environment marked by supply fragilities, inflation volatility and fragmented policy signals across central banks. In this update, we explore six global geoeconomic themes that are reshaping the outlook of the global economy.

### 1. Global reordering: policy-driven trade and geopolitical disruptions

Global trade is undergoing a profound transformation as policy becomes a disruptive force in shaping economic outcomes. The US administration’s sweeping tariffs on virtually all trading partners along with selective retaliation have reignited protectionist dynamics at a scale not seen in decades. The average US tariff rate surged from 2.5% at the end of 2024 to a peak of 29% in mid-April 2025, before easing to approximately 15% by early June following a reduction of China tariffs and temporary exemptions and exclusions.

 Abrupt policy shifts have injected a persistent fog of uncertainty over global trade flows while legal challenges to the new tariff regime have fueled protracted uncertainty over implementation timelines, exemptions, and the durability of current policies. This prolonged ambiguity is proving as disruptive as the tariffs themselves.

 Multinational firms are scrambling to adjust, delaying investment, reassessing supplier relationships and rerouting supply chains — all amid fluctuating cost structures and shifting market access. Financial markets have responded with heightened volatility as investors try to price in unpredictable and politically charged trade dynamics. The global repercussions are evident: input costs are rising, global trade volumes are slowing and traditional supply chain geographies are being reconfigured.

 In parallel, governments are responding with defensive measures — from retaliatory tariffs to strategic subsidies — amplifying the fragmentation of the global trade system. This evolution marks a departure from the rules-based order toward a more transactional and politicized global economy. In this new era of policy-driven volatility, agility in global strategy, supply chain resilience and trade risk management will be critical for business leaders navigating a less stable and more fractured economic landscape.

Tensions in the Middle East — evaluated across three scenarios developed in collaboration with EY’s Geostrategic Business Group — introduce substantial risks for financial markets, energy prices, and global trade flows. An escalation could amplify volatility in oil and commodity markets and disrupt key trade chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Suez Canal, triggering inflationary pressures, and posing serious challenges to global supply chains and economic stability.

### 2. Financial markets: repricing risk in a shifting landscape

Global financial markets are undergoing a fundamental shift, marked by the breakdown of long-standing correlations between asset classes. A striking example is the weakening of the US dollar despite rising Treasury yields — a decoupling that signals deepening investor unease about the US fiscal trajectory, rising public debt and escalating trade tensions.

 This reassessment is prompting a broader repricing of risk. Dollar-denominated assets, once viewed as safe havens, are now being re-evaluated, triggering a pivot toward global portfolio diversification. The softer dollar, while supporting export competitiveness for many emerging markets, is also amplifying currency volatility and complicating central bank policy choices across other regions.

 Meanwhile, equity markets appear to be pricing in a soft-landing scenario with surprising confidence, discounting the inflationary and growth-dampening effects of sustained tariff regimes. The persistence of policy-driven shocks — via trade, regulation and fiscal stimulus — is feeding into market dynamics that are increasingly disconnected from macroeconomic fundamentals. Against this backdrop, investors are adopting a more cautious and selective approach; reassessing asset valuations; and navigating a more fragmented, politically influenced global financial landscape.

### 3. Price volatility: inflation dynamics and supply chain fragilities

Inflation dynamics are being fundamentally reshaped by the resurgence of tariffs and the fragmentation of global trade. Unlike past episodes driven by demand booms or commodity cycles, today’s price volatility is increasingly policy induced — anchored in trade barriers that are redrawing cost structures and reshaping consumer prices.

 For economies imposing tariffs, most notably the US, these measures are acting as significant supply shocks, sharply raising input costs in sectors reliant on imported goods. Tariffs are also distorting resource allocation, forcing firms to reorient supply chains and investment decisions based on political and policy risk rather than cost efficiency. This shift is undermining productivity, particularly in trade-intensive industries, and weakening long-term competitiveness by diverting resources away from higher-value uses.

 Conversely, economies facing these tariffs — chiefly, major US trading partners — are confronting negative demand shocks. Reduced export volumes and elevated uncertainty are weighing on manufacturing activity, corporate revenues and employment. For these economies, the inflation effect moves in reverse: weakening demand exerts downward pressure on prices, amplifying disinflationary trends and, in some cases, raising deflation risks.

 In essence, trade policy has become a key vector for global inflation, challenging the conventional playbook for businesses and central banks. As tariff regimes evolve, and as legal battles and geopolitical frictions prolong the uncertainty, business leaders will continue to navigate a volatile, asymmetric, deeply political global pricing environment.

### 4. Monetary policy: cautious recalibration amid uncertainty

Global monetary policy is becoming increasingly fragmented as diverging inflation paths force central banks to recalibrate around shifting domestic priorities. Rather than responding to traditional demand-driven cycles, policymakers are contending with a volatile mix of tariffs, subsidies and supply shocks that are distorting price signals and complicating the inflation outlook.

 The Federal Reserve, after easing rates by 100 basis points in 2024, now faces a narrow policy path. Growth is softening, yet renewed inflationary pressure from tariffs and expansionary fiscal policy — both supply-side in nature — complicates the case for further rate cuts this year. The risk of holding rates too high for too long is rising. In Japan, the central bank is continuing its tightening cycle while the European Central Bank is tilting dovish, reacting to currency appreciation and subdued price pressures as well as bracing for the disinflationary impact of US tariffs. These divergent stances are amplifying exchange rate volatility, particularly as the US dollar weakens.

 Central banks across emerging markets are approaching policy recalibration with caution, navigating a complex mix of domestic and external pressures. While inflation is broadly moderating, the policy response remains uneven. Some central banks are pausing or reversing rate cuts in response to fiscal concerns or inflation persistence, while others are cautiously easing to support domestic demand.

 What ties these divergent approaches together is a heightened sensitivity to external volatility and risks. Tariff spillovers, geopolitical tensions and shifting capital flows are exerting growing influence over monetary decisions, prompting more defensive and risk-aware strategies.

### 5. Fiscal policy: navigating competing priorities

Fiscal policy is entering a more delicate phase as governments worldwide face mounting pressure to stimulate demand without undermining financial stability. In the US, the prospect of a widening fiscal deficit, driven by tax cut extensions and elevated interest costs, is raising alarms over debt sustainability. These dynamics are pushing long-term yields higher, with investors demanding greater compensation for rising fiscal and inflation risks. The result is a more challenging borrowing environment that risks crowding out private investment.

 Across developed markets, fiscal policy is being pulled in multiple directions. Governments are under pressure to sustain investment in long-term priorities — such as infrastructure, digitalization and the energy transition — while contending with limited fiscal space and rising demands for near-term relief. In Europe, fiscal policy is moving toward greater flexibility. Germany has eased its debt brake to accommodate increased defense and infrastructure spending while, at the EU level, proposals like Readiness 2030 reflect a push for collective investment in security in response to reduced US engagement. These shifts are contributing to higher public borrowing needs and rising term premiums, placing upward pressure on long-term interest rates.

 Emerging markets face stricter constraints. Elevated debt servicing costs, currency volatility and tighter global financing conditions are limiting fiscal headroom. Some, like India, continue to pursue targeted public investment to sustain growth, while others, particularly in Latin America, are grappling with investor concerns about fiscal discipline and long-term debt sustainability.

 The broader risk across economies is the gradual erosion of fiscal space. As debt service burdens grow, the ability to fund growth-enabling expenditures is shrinking. The imperative now is to design fiscal strategies that are stimulative and sustainable, anchored in credible frameworks that support long-term productivity without undermining market confidence.

### 6. Labor in flux: scarcity, skills and AI-driven productivity

Global labor markets are undergoing a structural transformation as firms respond to cost pressures, demographic constraints and shifting technology frontiers. Across developed markets and emerging economies, businesses are doubling down on efficiency — prioritizing training, automation and the deployment of generative AI to manage labor costs and enhance productivity.

 The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital tools is becoming a critical strategy for competitiveness. In the US, productivity gains have remained resilient even as wage growth has cooled, reflecting stronger business investment and improved workforce efficiency. In Europe and Japan, the challenge is more acute, with aging populations and rigid labor markets slowing adaptation. Meanwhile, emerging markets, particularly in Asia, are investing in digital infrastructure and workforce upskilling to seize demographic advantages and reduce dependence on labor-intensive models.

 Talent shortages will remain a persistent constraint, especially in sectors undergoing rapid digital transformation. Immigration policies, education systems and labor participation dynamics will all play a role in determining whether economies can harness or hinder this next phase of growth.

*   US
--

The US economy is expected to slow from 2.8% in 2024 to 1.5% in 2025 and 1.3% in 2026, as early-year strength — driven by front-loaded demand ahead of tariff hikes — fades and trade headwinds mount. Consumer spending and business investment are set to weaken in H2, with elevated uncertainty and tighter financial conditions weighing on sentiment. The labor market is cooling steadily, with job growth slowing, unemployment rising toward 5.0% and immigration policies further constraining labor supply. Tariffs will push inflation back above 3% by late 2025, though falling energy prices and demand softening will limit upside risks. Fiscal policy is expected to avoid a sharp contraction via the extension of expiring provisions from the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, but any stimulus will likely be modest and narrowly targeted, offering only a marginal tailwind. The Fed is expected to remain cautious through midyear and cut rates twice in September and December. Next year, the Fed is expected to ease the policy rate by another 100 basis points (bps) toward 3% as growth and labor conditions deteriorate.   Read more  Read less       
*   Canada
------

Canada’s economy entered 2025 with moderate momentum, but early strength driven by a surge in pre-tariff exports is fading, with GDP now at risk of contracting in midyear. Growth is projected to slow to 1.3% in 2025 and 0.7% in 2026, as trade uncertainty recedes and financial conditions ease. Inflation remains slightly above target, with tariff-related pressures partially offset by lower energy prices. The Bank of Canada has cut rates to 2.75%, with further easing expected through 2026. Labor market softening, elevated debt and weak productivity continue to weigh on demand, though easing rates and stabilizing inflation should support a gradual recovery, with GDP growth reaching 1.5% year over year (y/y) by Q4 2026.   Read more  Read less       
*   Euro area
---------

The euro area outlook remains moderately positive, with GDP expected to grow by 1.0% in 2025 and 1.3% in 2026, supported by recovering consumption and fiscal expansion in Germany. However, tariffs and policy uncertainty continue to weigh on exports and investment. Inflation has eased, with headline rates stabilizing near 2%, though core inflation — driven by services — remains slightly elevated. We expect core CPI to decline to 2.4% by late 2025 and converge toward 2% by 2026. In response to modest GDP growth, stable price pressures and global trade risks, the European Central Bank (ECB) reduced interest rates by 25bps at each meeting this year, bringing the deposit rate to 2% in June. We expect one more rate cut in September, with the deposit rate stabilizing at 1.75%.   Read more  Read less       
*   UK
--

The UK outlook remains subdued, with growth momentum expected to weaken through mid-2025 as tariff uncertainty and weak external demand weigh on business and consumer confidence. While the US-UK trade deal offers limited relief, GDP is forecast to expand by just 1.0% in both 2025 and 2026. Inflation remains elevated, with CPI likely to stay above 3% for most of 2025, driven by sticky domestic costs including utilities and wages. Tariff effects are expected to be modestly disinflationary, helped by lower energy prices and redirected imports from mainland China. The Bank of England is easing cautiously, with the Bank Rate forecast to fall to 3.75% by late 2025. However, fiscal policy faces growing strain, and with key decisions deferred to autumn, further tax rises or rule changes are increasingly likely.   Read more  Read less       
*   Japan
-----

Japan’s recovery remains modest, with GDP growth forecast at 0.7% in 2025. Private consumption is supported by rising wages and easing inflation, though uneven income gains and weak external demand are tempering momentum. Business investment is picking up slowly, while exports remain soft due to trade frictions. Inflation is projected to moderate from 3.8% in Q1 to 2.4% by year-end. The BoJ is expected to continue gradual tightening, with the policy rate reaching 1% by early 2026.   Read more  Read less       
*   Australia
---------

Australia’s economy is regaining momentum, with growth projected to rise from 1.0% in 2024 to 1.9% in 2025, aided by rate cuts, improving household consumption and temporary tax relief. Labor market conditions remain resilient, though some softening is expected. Inflation has returned to the Reserve Bank of Australia’s 2%–3% range, enabling further easing. However, external risks from global trade tensions and tariffs pose a downside risk to exports and confidence.   Read more  Read less       
*   China
-----

China’s economy is expected to grow 4.4% in 2025, down from 5.0% in 2024, as weak consumer demand, sluggish investment and trade tensions weigh on momentum. Fiscal policy is set to turn more expansionary in H2 2025, with a renewed focus on boosting domestic demand and infrastructure investment. The People’s Bank of China is likely to maintain an accommodative stance, targeting support to housing, strategic sectors and small firms. While tariff escalation risks will likely be contained, existing tariffs and non-tariff trade measures such as export controls are expected to rise.   Read more  Read less       
*   India
-----

India’s economy is expected to maintain solid momentum, with GDP growth at 6.6% in 2025, supported by resilient services exports, steady public investment and robust rural demand. Risks persist on the external front due to US trade measures, while manufacturing remains subdued. Inflation is moderating toward the RBI’s 4% mid-point target, allowing for 50bps of rate cuts this year, contingent on global conditions.   Read more  Read less       
*   Latin America
-------------

The growth outlook for Latin America remains modest, with regional GDP expected to expand by around 2.2% in 2025 after a 2.0% pace in 2024. Argentina is forecast to rebound strongly from recession amid policy stabilization, while Brazil is set to slow as tighter monetary conditions and weak external demand weigh on investment. Mexico faces stagnation due to spillovers from US tariffs and policy uncertainty. Inflation has eased but remains above target in several economies, prompting central banks to delay further easing. Debt vulnerabilities and limited fiscal space continue to constrain policy flexibility across much of the region.   Read more  Read less       
*   ASEAN
-----

ASEAN’s growth outlook remains broadly positive, with GDP projected to expand by 4.5% in 2025, supported by resilient domestic demand, a rebound in tourism and strengthening electronics exports. However, escalating US-China trade tensions and rising US tariffs pose a growing risk, particularly for export-dependent and manufacturing-led economies, where external headwinds could weigh on activity and dampen investor sentiment. Meanwhile, ongoing structural reforms, deeper regional integration and recent upgrades to trade agreements are bolstering competitiveness and attracting investment. Inflation is easing across most member economies, providing central banks with policy space to support growth if needed.   Read more  Read less       
*   Middle East and North Africa
----------------------------

Growth in the MENA region is expected to accelerate to 3.6% in 2025, up from 1.9% in 2024, supported by a rebound in oil output, rising investment and improving regional demand. The recent US-GCC (Gulf Cooperation Council) summit yielded multiple trade and investment agreements, reinforcing the region’s long-term diversification drive, particularly in AI and technology. Inflation is moderating region-wide, falling from 6.4% in 2024 to 4.3% in 2025, led by Egypt. In contrast, GCC inflation will rise modestly to 2.1%, reflecting higher housing and service costs. Monetary policy is expected to remain tight across most of the region, with Egypt initiating rate cuts and the GCC holding rates broadly stable.   Read more  Read less       
*   Sub-Saharan Africa
------------------

SSA is projected to grow 3.1% in 2025, up from 3.0% in 2024, with easing inflation and looser policy aiding recovery. Growth remains uneven, with service-led economies performing better than commodity-dependent peers. Inflation is expected to fall from 18.1% to 13.4%, creating room for selective rate cuts. Key risks include climate shocks, security concerns and tighter external financing conditions.   Read more  Read less

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

In a year marked by policy fluidity, economic desynchronization and supply fragilities, business leaders should prioritize two core imperatives to achieve sustainable performance and shock resistance:

1.   Agility and adaptability for strategic resilience: Navigate complexity by embedding flexible planning frameworks that allow for rapid recalibration. Develop scenario-based strategies that incorporate geopolitical shifts, trade disruptions and regulatory swings. Embrace modular operations, responsive pricing and cross-functional coordination to adjust to diverging market conditions across regions and sectors.

2.   Shock absorption and structural robustness:Reinforce the organization’s capacity to weather volatility by strengthening supply networks, diversifying input sources, and investing in robust digital and operational infrastructure. Focus on cost discipline, liquidity management and workforce resilience — while leveraging productivity gains from AI and automation to mitigate the impact of renewed inflationary or financial shocks.

Key Takeaways
=============

*   Global activity has been stronger than we expected, but growth drivers are narrowing, and the U.S. labor market is clearly weakening. Oil prices and data centers are bright spots.
*   Financial conditions remain supportive as asset prices are high, bond yields have declined, spreads are tight, and the Fed delivered its first rate cut of the year in September.
*   We raised our 2025 GDP growth forecasts on base effects, although the narrative of weaker activity over our forecast horizon is still valid as long as policy uncertainty remains high.
*   Our risks tilt toward the downside and include a harder-than-expected U.S. landing and structurally higher borrowing rates leading to deteriorating debt dynamics. 

U.S. policy uncertainty, while declining, continues to hang over the global macro picture. U.S. tariffs and policies more generally dominate discussions with our clients and stakeholders and remain front and center in our credit conditions forecasting exercise.

We continue to believe that sustained policy uncertainty "leaves money on the table." This is because investment, discretionary consumer spending, and hence employment and output, are lower than they otherwise would be. Policy uncertainties more than the policies themselves are moving the macro needle.

#### Resilience Is Not Quite Dead

Recent global macro data has been somewhat stronger than we expected. This includes national accounts data for the second quarter for many economies. While part of this outperformance can be explained as the payback for a volatile first half due to front-running of U.S. import tariffs, the post-pandemic resilience continues to shine through.

Balance sheets for corporates and households remain healthy, supporting spending, particularly on services. Near full employment of labor buttresses this result.

The soft data have improved as well. We had previously identified a gap between the soft, survey-based data and the hard, activity-based data. The former had been flashing weaker signals than the latter. However, this gap has been closing as purchasing managers indices in August have improved. We have seen some improvements in European investor confidence and US manufacturing sentiment as well.

A major data event since our last quarterly report has been the softening of the U.S. labor market. The pace of job creation, net of revisions has fallen to 22,000 a month over the past three months, down from 123,000 per month average over the first four months of the year.

Moreover, U.S. job gains have narrowed, with only the healthcare sector adding workers. Manufacturing employment has fallen this year and federal government employment has declined, reflecting cuts by the administration. Elsewhere, labor market outcomes are broadly stable, with unemployment rates near estimates of longer-run steady state.

#### Some Upsides Emerge

On the positive side, global oil prices continue to decline. The market is oversupplied, aggravated by the recent increasing in output by OPEC+. Chinese restocking has partly blunted downward price pressures in recent quarters, but this factor should ease, putting more downward pressure on prices.

Lower oil prices are boosting household and industry demand, particularly in the emerging markets, where oil has a higher weight in consumption baskets and industrial oil intensity to GDP is higher. These demand tailwinds outweigh downside pressure on oil producers.

Another positive macro factor is the rise of data centers. This development mainly affects the U.S. and China, which have entered an AI race, although this trend is harder to identify in the Chinese data. For the U.S., non-data center investment spending has been weak this year, reflecting a necessary slowdown, aggravated by policy uncertainty.

However, data center construction, equipment and power requirements have lifted non-residential investment growth to 8% annualized over the first half of the year, contributing about 1 percentage point to GDP growth. While questions remain around the long-term growth and productivity impacts of AI, the construction phase is clearly growth-positive for now.

Buoyant asset prices via the wealth effect have also supported spending. Equity prices are at or near all-time highs in many jurisdictions following a strong second quarter earnings season and a healthy near-term earnings outlook. Relief over the more modest than expected effects of tariffs on activity has also helped.

Housing price growth looks more mixed as higher borrowing rates are eroding demand. However, price levels remain high particularly where the supply response has been weaker. Affordability remains a concern for new home buyers.

#### Inflation And Policy Rates

Inflation is grinding higher in the U.S. as tariffs pass through, although at a slower pace than we previously thought. U.S. August consumer price index core inflation rose to 3.1% and producer price index inflation rose to 2.8%. Services inflation is close to 4%. Elsewhere, eurozone inflation is at the 2% target.

The U.S. Federal Reserve cut rates for the first time this year in September, taking the policy rate 25 basis points lower to 4.00%-4.25%. The move was widely anticipated following the recent weakness in labor market data, although the recent uptick in inflation complicated the assessment.

In its statement, the Fed focused more on its full employment mandate and is looking through the tariff-induced rise in inflation, given that medium-term inflation expectations remain well-anchored.

Elsewhere in central banks, the European Central Bank (ECB) held rates as expected as their rates are in neutral territory, and the Bank of England is on hold as wage and price pressures remain elevated. The central banks of Australia and Canada cut policy rates at the latest meetings in August and September, respectively. Overall, developed market central banks continue to cut cautiously, mostly in 25-basis point (bps) intervals.

In contrast, emerging market central banks have been lowering rates at a quicker pace, reflecting both lower oil prices and the benefit of stronger currencies lowering import prices. They also have more scope to cut since in many cases real policy rates were raised to higher levels than in developed market central banks.

The U.S. dollar has weakened modestly since the U.S. election in early November 2024. The well-known U.S. Dollar Index (DXY) shows the dollar is now down by about 4% overall since the election and 8% peak-to-trough.

The greenback's performance has differed noticeably against other counties/regions. The dollar has fallen by more than 10% against the euro and yen but has actually strengthened modestly against the Indian rupee. The dollar has fallen against many emerging market currencies, helping to contain imported inflation in those economies.

#### Growth Forecasts Have Nudged Higher On Stronger Q2 Growth

We have raised our growth outlook modestly since our last quarterly report. Most of the revision comes from a stronger second quarter base effect and does not reflect a brighter outlook.

We now see slightly higher GDP growth in all major economies in 2025. We raised our U.S. forecast by 20 bps, the eurozone by 30 bps, and China by 30 bps. We also have higher growth in Japan and Mexico, for similar reasons.

Canada is the outlier, where we have marked growth lower by 30 bps due to the effects of U.S. tariffs. Global growth climbs back above 3% this year following our latest revisions.

#### Regional Updates

[](https://www.spglobal.com/ratings/en/regulatory/article/global-economic-outlook-q4-2025-global-resilience-battles-us-policy-unpredictability-s101647254)
##### U.S.

Our higher growth forecast largely reflects multiple factors:

*   Better economic activity than we expected since our previous forecast. 
*   The reconciliation act's slight boost to private sector activity and federal defense spending, and the diminishing effects of uncertainty about U.S. trade policy.
*   The impact of lower net immigration on aggregate demand and the labor supply is a key headwind to near-term growth whereas ongoing large amounts of high-tech investment is a tailwind.

The cooling of the labor market while inflation remains sticky above target has the Fed in a bind. In the near term, we expect the Fed to emphasize downside risks to full employment and continue easing gradually (25bps per meeting) over the next quarter, thus bringing the Fed funds rate to 3.6% by year-end 2025. We anticipate rates to settle at 3.1% by late 2026.

For details, see "[Economic Outlook U.S. Q4 2025: Below-Trend Growth Persists Amid A Swirl Of Policy Shifts](https://www.spglobal.com/ratings/en/regulatory/article/-/view/sourceId/101646549)," published on Sept. 23, 2025.

##### Eurozone

A host of uncertainties weigh on eurozone growth this year, but conditions for accelerating GDP growth beyond 2025 remain. Support will come from lower policy rates, a strong labor market, and German fiscal stimulus, consistent with projected eurozone growth above potential by mid-2026.

Low consumer confidence holds back recovery in some countries, although the recovery has begun and we expect it to strengthen further over our forecast horizon. Sticky inflation in services reflects the ongoing strength of the labor market, suggesting the ECB is done with rate cuts unless new external shocks emerge. In this context, the rapid appreciation of the euro is a factor to monitor.

For details, see "[Economic Outlook Eurozone Q4 2025: Recovery Continues Despite Consumer Hesitancy](https://www.spglobal.com/ratings/en/regulatory/article/-/view/sourceId/101645506)," Sept. 23, 2025.

[](https://www.spglobal.com/ratings/en/regulatory/article/global-economic-outlook-q4-2025-global-resilience-battles-us-policy-unpredictability-s101647254)
##### China/Asia-Pacific

We expect China's economy to slow to about 4% year-on-year in the second half of 2025 and 2026. This view reflects weakening exports, tepid organic domestic demand, and contained macro stimulus. We don't see downward pressure on prices easing soon.

Across the region, relatively resilient domestic demand should dampen the impact from stronger external headwinds following the increase in U.S. import tariffs and slower global growth. Inflation is easing and currencies have strengthened against the U.S. dollar. With U.S. policy rates likely to come down more and policymakers looking to support growth, many central banks are likely to cut policy interest rates some more.

For details, see "[Economic Outlook Asia-Pacific Q4 2025: Growth To Ease On External Strain](https://www.spglobal.com/ratings/en/regulatory/article/-/view/sourceId/101645760)," Sept. 22, 2025.

[](https://www.spglobal.com/ratings/en/regulatory/article/global-economic-outlook-q4-2025-global-resilience-battles-us-policy-unpredictability-s101647254)
##### Emerging markets

Our baseline narrative is broadly unchanged because we still expect trade to soften in the coming quarters. This as the frontloading of U.S. imports that took place in the first half of 2025 unwinds. The magnitude of the trade slowdown is highly uncertain and its impact on emerging markets will vary.

Resilient domestic demand and favorable financial conditions, helped by continued U.S. dollar weakness and lower central bank policy rates, will partly offset weakness in trade flows. The resumption of Fed easing will likely encourage several emerging market central banks to continue lowering interest rates, although the space for further interest rate cuts is likely to be limited, as many of those central banks have been reducing policy rates for more than a year.

For details, see "[Economic Outlook Emerging Markets Q4 2025: Tariff Impact Still Looms](https://www.spglobal.com/ratings/en/regulatory/article/-/view/sourceId/101646248)," Sept. 23, 2025.

#### Risks To Our Baseline

The main global macro risk we see is a sharp deterioration in the U.S. labor market, leading to a U.S. recession and its spillovers. While our baseline already contains a pronounced slowdown in the pace of U.S. growth (with a trough of about 1% in the fourth quarter of 2025) and a moderate rise in unemployment (to more than 4.5% in early 2026), recent labor market data suggest things could get worse.

We have documented the narrowness of U.S. job growth and the decline in labor market churn seen in both gross hirings and firings. Together, these point to lower resilience and put the labor market on a more fragile footing.

Another policy or confidence shock could push the U.S. economy into recession, with the associated material drop in U.S. demand spilling over to trading partners directly and economies with strong U.S. financial linkages less directly.

Another risk is a sharp rise in global interest rates. This could reflect some combination of higher perceived creditworthiness or policy uncertainty, higher debt levels, and higher investment demand.

This would be especially pernicious if the change in interest rates (r) is larger than a change in growth (g). This is because of the importance of (r-g) in debt dynamics: a higher value implies a stronger primary fiscal outturn is required just to keep debt-to-GDP levels constant.

We have passed through a long period where (r-g) has been low or even negative. This has given rise to heavy borrowing on the assumption that levels of (r-g) would continue. That does not appear to be the case, raising the specter of credit market stress, with the associated macro fallout.

Our upside risks would be the continuation of the two recent growth enhancing surprises:

Sustained, moderately lower oil prices This development would put sustained higher purchasing power into household and energy using firms, boosting growth. Lower oil prices have favorable global distributional effects as well since lower income countries spend a higher share of their income on energy. The supply side (oil producers) would need to adjust, but we agree with the conventional wisdom that, on net, lower oil prices are good for growth since consumers spend more than producers. We would underscore that this upside risk related to moderately lower prices. If prices go too low, then the outcome would be negative, as we saw in 2015.

Broader, deeper data center build-out The rise of data centers takes us into unfamiliar territory since the tech firms driving the build-out have traditionally been light on capital expenditure. The AI race aspect does raise risks of a construction bubble, but an acceleration of the near-term build-out will boost growth, with construction possible spreading outside the U.S., and benefit the producers of data center inputs. The ultimate upside is a sustained, strong rise in growth-boosting productivity.

#### Waving The Magic Wand

Finally, our aspirational "magic wand" outcome would be a return to the historic norm of negligible U.S. policy uncertainty. Abrupt policy changes--including tariffs and related industrial policy actions--can be absorbed by the markets once agents are convinced that no further changes or negotiations are forthcoming.

Markets will re-price, portfolios will adjust, resource re-allocation will take place if required. Separately, supply-side reforms such as tax policy, more sensible regulation, and permitting reform will kick in.

This will set the stage for healthy growth. But low policy uncertainty would need to be sustained, implying a material change in the U.S. operating model. Absent that, our fear is that the negative overhang on growth will continue.
